article_content: A leading Muslim-American civil rights organization is calling for stronger grassroots collaboration between police and Muslim communities to help thwart homegrown terrorism. Released on Friday by the Muslim Public Affairs Council, the report 'Building Bridges to Strengthen America: Forging an Effective Counterterrorism Enterprise between Muslim Americans and Law Enforcement' details the alarm felt by American Muslims after incidents like the Fort Hood shooting, the arrests of five American Muslims in Pakistan, and the arrests of eight Somali-American men accused of attempting to recruit youths for a Somali rebel movement. The 32-page paper underscores the need for a shared approach: law enforcement agencies should focus on criminal activity, including terrorism, while Muslim community leaders work to address the social and ideological factors that can lead to radicalization. Both groups, the report says, must coordinate their efforts to build trust and address security concerns effectively. 'We will capture the narrative from those who seek to misguide young people,' said Haris Tarin, director of the council's Washington, D.C., office, at a news conference introducing the report. 'One incident of violent extremism is one too many,' added the report's author, Alejandro J. Beutel, who serves as the council's government liaison. He also emphasized the importance of community policing, in which local residents work closely with officers who understand the cultural and linguistic nuances of the neighborhood. The study notes that distrust of law enforcement is a significant hurdle in many communities. Spying on peaceful activists, monitoring houses of worship without reasonable suspicion, and religious profiling can deepen this distrust. Such actions, according to the report, may also fuel grievances that extremists can exploit. Tarin and Beutel stressed that addressing radicalization concerns within Muslim communities is not new; many have been actively discussing these issues for years. They urged Muslim leaders to stay engaged with youth in social and digital spaces, remain vigilant against radical ideologies, and work together across different Muslim groups. Beutel noted that American Muslims can learn from British experiences following the 2005 London bombings, when alienation and social pressures were identified as major factors driving radicalism. Implementing better religious education and social outreach, according to Beutel, is key to preventing extremism and aiding law enforcement. 'Muslim communities must do their part to reach out and assist law enforcement in bringing real terrorist perpetrators to justice,' he wrote.

Ce document de 32 pages souligne la nécessité d'une approche partagée : les forces de l'ordre doivent se concentrer sur la criminalité, y compris le terrorisme, tandis que les dirigeants communautaires travaillent sur les facteurs sociaux et idéologiques menant à la radicalisation. Les deux parties, indique le rapport, doivent coordonner leurs efforts pour instaurer un climat de confiance et résoudre efficacement les problèmes de sécurité. 'Nous allons reprendre le récit à ceux qui cherchent à mal orienter les jeunes', a déclaré Haris Tarin, directeur du bureau de l'organisation à Washington (D.C.), lors d'une conférence de presse présentant le rapport. 'Un seul incident d'extrémisme violent, c'est déjà trop', a ajouté l'auteur du rapport, Alejandro J. Beutel, chargé des relations gouvernementales de l'organisation. Il a également insisté sur l'importance de la police de proximité, où les résidents locaux collaborent étroitement avec des agents qui comprennent les nuances culturelles et linguistiques de la communauté. L'étude note que la méfiance envers la police constitue un obstacle majeur dans de nombreuses communautés. La surveillance d'activistes pacifiques, la mise sous surveillance de lieux de culte sans motif raisonnable et le profilage religieux peuvent renforcer cette méfiance. De telles pratiques, selon le rapport, alimentent également des griefs dont les extrémistes peuvent tirer parti. Tarin et Beutel ont souligné que la question de la radicalisation au sein des communautés musulmanes n'est pas nouvelle ; beaucoup la discutent activement depuis des années. Ils ont appelé les dirigeants musulmans à rester engagés auprès des jeunes dans les espaces sociaux et numériques, à se montrer vigilants face aux idéologies radicales et à coopérer entre différents groupes musulmans. Beutel a noté que les musulmans américains peuvent tirer des leçons de l'expérience britannique après les attentats de Londres en 2005, où l'isolement et les pressions sociales ont été identifiés comme des facteurs importants de radicalisation. Mettre en place une meilleure éducation religieuse et un meilleur engagement social est essentiel, selon Beutel, pour prévenir l'extrémisme et aider les forces de l'ordre. 'Les communautés musulmanes doivent faire leur part pour se rapprocher et aider les forces de l'ordre à traduire en justice les véritables auteurs d'actes terroristes', a-t-il écrit.

article_content: The White House inadvertently shared the identity of the CIA's leading intelligence officer in Afghanistan with thousands of reporters. This individual was included on a roster of attendees at a military briefing for President Barack Obama during his unannounced trip to Bagram Airfield on Sunday. Normally, the media is given attendee lists, but identifying intelligence officers is highly unusual. In this instance, the officer's name was listed beside 'Chief of Station,' drawing significant attention. A print pool reporter copied the provided list and circulated it through standard press channels. Scott Wilson of The Washington Post later spotted the mistake and alerted the White House, which then distributed a revised list omitting the station chief's identity. Privately, officials expressed alarm but have not commented publicly about the incident. A station chief oversees the CIA's operations in a foreign nation, coordinating with local intelligence services. They remain anonymous to safeguard covert work and personal safety. CNN withheld the individual's name due to potential danger. Valerie Plame, a former CIA operative famously exposed in the Bush era, called this error 'astonishing.'

article_content: 'On Tuesday, Japan once more issued an apology to South Korea for its decades-long control of the Korean peninsula in the early 1900s.' 'This renewed message accompanies the 100th anniversary of Japan’s formal annexation of Korea, though it is not the first such statement.' 'Prime Minister Naoto Kan voiced his profound regret for the hardships caused under Japanese rule, and the cabinet backed his remarks, according to Japanese media.' 'Kan also pledged to return valuable Korean cultural items that South Korea has been asking for, including records from an ancient royal dynasty.' 'Between 1910 and 1945, Japan governed Korea. During that period, the Japanese military reportedly forced around 200,000 women, predominantly Korean and Chinese, into sexual servitude under the label of comfort women.' 'South Korea has a history of protests and legal actions concerning these women’s suffering. While the ruling Grand National Party welcomed Kan’s statement as progress, it insisted that the apology did not fully address Korea’s grievances.' 'They highlighted that the statement fails to acknowledge the forced nature of annexation and the plight of those coerced into sex slavery or hard labor.'

'Le Premier ministre Naoto Kan a exprimé ses profonds regrets pour les souffrances causées sous la domination japonaise, et le cabinet a soutenu ses remarques, selon les médias japonais.' 'Kan a également promis de restituer des objets culturels coréens précieux que la Corée du Sud réclamait, dont des archives d’une ancienne dynastie royale.' 'De 1910 à 1945, le Japon a gouverné la Corée. Pendant cette période, l’armée japonaise aurait forcé environ 200 000 femmes, principalement coréennes et chinoises, à servir de prostituées sous le nom de femmes de réconfort.' 'La Corée du Sud a un passé de manifestations et d’actions en justice à propos des souffrances de ces femmes. Bien que le Grand Parti national au pouvoir ait salué la déclaration de Kan comme un progrès, il a souligné que les excuses ne traitent pas pleinement les griefs de la Corée.' 'Ils ont souligné que la déclaration ne reconnaît pas la nature forcée de l’annexion ni la situation de ceux qui ont été contraints à l’esclavage sexuel ou au travail forcé.'

article_content: Two former Care Quality Commission executives, Jill Finney and Anna Jefferson, insist they never sought to hide their roles in a contested internal report concerning a flawed hospital inspection at Furness General Hospital. Both say they advocated for openness, despite allegations that they attempted to shield the critical findings. Their identities were initially redacted, replaced with 'Mr G' and 'Mr F,' over privacy or legal concerns. Yet the move sparked claims of systemic concealment, forcing the CQC to publicly identify Finney, Jefferson, and then-Chief Executive Cynthia Bower. Finney, who lost her job following the controversy, and Jefferson, who is on maternity leave, believe the anonymity attempt only intensified public focus. Finney criticizes how the report was released, arguing it magnified media attention, while Jefferson calls the redaction a poor decision from the outset. They deny having suppressed the internal review into the Morecambe Bay NHS Foundation Trust. That trust included Furness General Hospital, where deaths among mothers and infants had raised alarm. Although the CQC ultimately launched an investigation, questions persist over the delay. Grant Thornton, an external consultancy, claimed senior CQC officials suppressed the report highlighting the CQC's failings. But Finney and Jefferson insist the document was not sufficiently critical of the watchdog, arguing hospital management held primary responsibility. Jefferson labels the review a 'whitewash,' not a revelatory document. They also reject suggestions that they directed the report's deletion to sidestep Freedom of Information laws. Jefferson notes she pressed for a deeper, external review, while Finney maintains no order was given to destroy the files, only that more work was required. Lawyers are examining possible actions against former CQC leaders, including pension-related consequences. Meanwhile, an MP has asked the Metropolitan Police to investigate the alleged cover-up, and Cumbria Police continue inquiries into one infant's death under the trust's care. Jefferson is scheduled to return from maternity leave soon, with her future role at the CQC uncertain.

article_content: A single chromosome can determine many differences between the sexes: the Y chromosome. Scientists have long theorized that the X and Y chromosomes were once identical, until the Y began to evolve. The exact timeline was unclear, but a Swiss research team now claims that mammalian sex genes emerged about 180 million years ago, potentially driven by global temperature changes. Another group of researchers found that, despite significant genetic decay, the Y chromosome has held onto a small cluster of genes that have been vital for male survival. Many of these genes do not directly affect sex determination or sperm production but may play a crucial role in how men and women differ in susceptibility to certain diseases. A study published in the journal Nature, led by researchers from the University of Lausanne’s Swiss Institute of Bioinformatics, analyzed Y chromosome genes from the three main mammal lineages: placentals (including humans, apes, rodents, and elephants), marsupials (such as opossums and kangaroos), and monotremes (egg-laying mammals such as the platypus and echidna). They also examined chicken DNA for comparison. Instead of sequencing the Y chromosomes directly, scientists compared genetic sequences from male and female tissues, eliminating common elements to isolate Y-specific sequences. This approach created the largest gene atlas of the male chromosome to date. They found that the SRY gene, key for testicular development in placentals and marsupials, appeared about 180 million years ago in a common ancestor. Meanwhile, the AMHY gene, present in monotremes, emerged approximately 175 million years ago. Both genes arose independently but at nearly the same time, suggesting environmental influences—possibly temperature—may have led to these genetic shifts.

Le calendrier exact restait incertain, mais une équipe de chercheurs suisses affirme maintenant que les gènes sexuels des mammifères sont apparus il y a environ 180 millions d’années, probablement sous l’influence de changements de température à l’échelle mondiale. Un autre groupe de chercheurs a découvert que, malgré une importante dégradation génétique, le chromosome Y a conservé un petit ensemble de gènes essentiels à la survie masculine. Nombre de ces gènes n’interviennent pas directement dans la détermination du sexe ou la production de spermatozoïdes, mais ils pourraient jouer un rôle crucial dans la façon dont hommes et femmes diffèrent en matière de sensibilité à certaines maladies. Une étude publiée dans la revue Nature, dirigée par des chercheurs de l’Institut Suisse de Bioinformatique de l’Université de Lausanne, a analysé les gènes du chromosome Y appartenant aux trois principales lignées de mammifères: les placentaires (y compris les humains, les singes, les rongeurs et les éléphants), les marsupiaux (comme les opossums et les kangourous) et les monotrèmes (mammifères pondeurs comme l’ornithorynque et l’échidné). Cette méthode a permis de constituer l’atlas génique le plus complet du chromosome mâle à ce jour. Ils ont découvert que le gène SRY, essentiel au développement testiculaire chez les placentaires et les marsupiaux, est apparu il y a environ 180 millions d’années chez un ancêtre commun. De son côté, le gène AMHY, présent chez les monotrèmes, est apparu il y a environ 175 millions d’années. Les deux gènes auraient émergé de façon indépendante, mais presque à la même époque, suggérant que des facteurs environnementaux — possiblement la température — pourraient avoir déclenché ces changements génétiques.

article_content: 'Eritrean asylum seekers who fled persecution and compulsory military conscription in one of the world's most repressive countries now face new hardships in Israel following a surprise attack by Hamas. Approximately 18,000 Eritreans reside in Israel, having escaped oppression in East Africa.' 'After an air strike hit southern Israel, Eritrean asylum seekers told the BBC about renewed displacement. Teklit, who has lived in the southern city of Ashkelon for 13 years, said his home was totally destroyed by a Hamas rocket on Sunday night. He described day-long shelling and noted that they usually receive evacuation alerts, but none arrived before this incident.' 'Another Eritrean described feeling like a new refugee after fleeing Ashkelon for the safer city of Netanya. He told the BBC that his house was destroyed, leaving him temporarily free from the terrible noise. Eritrean refugee rights activist, Berhane Negassi, who resides in Jerusalem, confirmed that no Eritrean fatalities have been reported, though some asylum seekers remain missing.' 'Israel is still reeling from the weekend attack, which killed more than 1,300 people. Daily life has been disrupted, with schools closed and many employees told not to work. Mr Negassi, who leads the Eritrean New Hope Organisation, explained that many Eritreans view Israel as a second home and cannot bear seeing it in such distress.' 'Life is particularly difficult for refugees facing single parenthood, health challenges, or financial troubles. Eritreans and Sudanese began arriving in Israel around 2006 via Egypt's Sinai Peninsula. In 2020, Israel granted asylum to fewer than 0.1% of applicants. The war between Israel and Hamas continues, with more than 2,300 people killed in Israel's retaliatory bombing of Gaza, and thousands of Palestinians fleeing from the north to the south of the territory.'

Yet no one discusses alternative platforms supposedly crushed by media campaigns, raising suspicions of deliberate suppression.' Still, unpredictable regulators may shut down any cross-chain function under claims of security, pushing the narrative of 'compliance vs. freedom.''
